## The Auxiliary Load-Balancing Loss {#sec-load-balancing-loss}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Sources for this section"}

| # | Source | Summary |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | [Fedus et al., "Switch Transformers," JMLR 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961) | The canonical $f_i \cdot P_i$ auxiliary loss formulation (Equations 2-4). |
| 2 | [Shazeer et al., "The Sparsely-Gated MoE Layer," ICLR 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.06538) | Original importance loss and load loss. |
| 3 | [Qiu et al., "Demons in the Detail: On Implementing Load Balancing Loss," 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.11873) | Micro-batch vs global-batch LBL matters hugely. |

:::

You now know how the router works: a linear projection, a top-k selection, and a softmax over survivors. You know that gradients flow through the softmax weights of the selected experts, but that non-selected experts sit in a gradient dead zone. In principle, this is enough for the forward pass to work. Tokens get routed, experts produce outputs, the model trains. So what goes wrong?

Everything. Without intervention, MoE training collapses into a degenerate state where a single expert hogs nearly all tokens while the others wither. The model ends up using a tiny fraction of its capacity. This section explains why that happens, how the field solved it, and why the solution is one of the most elegant tricks in modern deep learning.

### Expert Collapse: The Self-Reinforcing Death Spiral

Imagine a restaurant with four chefs, each capable of cooking any dish on the menu. On the first night, Chef 3 happens to cook a slightly better risotto than the others, perhaps because of random weight initialization. The head waiter, noticing this, sends the next risotto order to Chef 3 as well. Chef 3 gets more practice making risotto, improves further, and soon the waiter is routing *all* risotto orders to Chef 3. Then the pasta orders follow, because Chef 3 has now been cooking so often that they have gotten better at everything. Before long, Chef 3 is handling 80% of all orders while Chefs 1, 2, and 4 stand idle, their skills atrophying from disuse.

The dynamic just described is *expert collapse*, the single most dangerous failure mode in MoE training. The cycle is self-reinforcing:

1. Expert 3 starts slightly better for some tokens (due to random initialization)
2. The router sends more tokens to Expert 3
3. Expert 3 receives more gradient updates, improves further
4. The router, observing Expert 3's improved performance, sends even more tokens
5. Expert 3 now handles 80% of all tokens; Experts 1, 2, and 4 receive almost no gradients and stagnate

The result: a model with $N$ experts that behaves as if it has one expert. You paid for $N$ sets of parameters but are using one. The entire premise of MoE (decoupling capacity from compute) is destroyed.

![Expert collapse in action: the same set of experts is chosen across all 8 MoE layers regardless of the input, leaving other experts untrained. Source: Maarten Grootendorst, "A Visual Guide to Mixture of Experts" (2024).](Mixture of Experts/images/grootendorst-expert-collapse.png){#fig-expert-collapse-visual}

The feedback loop is the same "rich get richer" dynamic you see across many systems: social media algorithms that amplify already-popular content, urban economies where jobs concentrate in cities that already have jobs, academic citation counts that snowball because highly-cited papers attract more citations. Without a corrective force, positive feedback loops converge to winner-take-all outcomes.

### Shazeer's Original Approach (2017)

The first serious attempt at preventing expert collapse came from [Shazeer et al. (ICLR 2017)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.06538). They introduced two separate penalty terms.

The first was the *importance loss*. For a batch of tokens $X$, define the *importance* of expert $i$ as the total gate weight it receives across the batch:

$$
\text{Importance}(X)_i = \sum_{x \in X} G(x)_i
$$

The importance loss penalizes unequal importance by minimizing the squared coefficient of variation:

$$
L_{\text{importance}} = w_{\text{importance}} \cdot \text{CV}(\text{Importance}(X))^2
$$

The coefficient of variation (standard deviation divided by mean) is zero when all experts have equal total gate weight, and positive otherwise. The importance loss encourages the router to distribute its softmax mass evenly. But there is a subtle gap: equal total gate weight does not guarantee equal token counts. One expert could receive huge gate weights on a few tokens (high importance), while another receives small gate weights on many tokens (also high importance). The number of tokens per expert can still be wildly unbalanced.

To address this gap, Shazeer added a separate *load loss* (described in the paper's appendix) that more directly targets the token count distribution. The full formulation involved a smooth approximation to the discrete assignment counts, using the cumulative distribution function of the noise added to the logits. It was effective but complex.

### The Switch Transformer Formulation: $f_i \times P_i$

[Fedus et al. (JMLR 2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961) simplified everything into a single, clean loss function. The Switch Transformer formulation has become the standard. It is built from two quantities, each measured across a batch $\mathcal{B}$ of $T$ tokens and $N$ experts.

The first quantity is $f_i$, the *dispatch fraction*: the fraction of tokens in the batch that were actually routed to expert $i$.

$$
f_i = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{x \in \mathcal{B}} \mathbb{1}\{\text{argmax}\; p(x) = i\}
$$ {#eq-fi}

Here $\mathbb{1}\{\cdot\}$ is the *indicator function*, which returns 1 when its condition is true and 0 otherwise. The quantity $f_i$ is a count. If 4 out of 8 tokens in the batch go to expert $i$, then $f_i = 0.5$. Because this is defined through an argmax and an indicator function, $f_i$ is **not differentiable**. You cannot compute $\partial f_i / \partial \theta$ for any router parameter $\theta$, because the indicator function has zero gradient almost everywhere and is undefined at the decision boundary.

The second quantity is $P_i$, the *probability fraction*: the average router probability allocated to expert $i$ across the batch.

$$
P_i = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{x \in \mathcal{B}} p_i(x)
$$ {#eq-pi}

Here $p_i(x)$ is the softmax probability that the router assigns to expert $i$ for token $x$. The quantity $P_i$ is a smooth function of the router weights. You can differentiate through softmax. So $P_i$ **is differentiable**.

The auxiliary load-balancing loss is the dot product of these two vectors, scaled:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = \alpha \cdot N \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{N} f_i \cdot P_i
$$ {#eq-aux-loss}

That is the entire formulation. Three lines of math. But the insight packed into this product is deep, and understanding *why* it works is the intellectual core of this chapter.

::: {.exercise-predict correct="C"}

Before reading the next subsection, make a prediction. The auxiliary loss uses two quantities: the dispatch fraction $f_i$ (the actual fraction of tokens sent to each expert) and the probability fraction $P_i$ (the average softmax probability per expert). If you could only track ONE of these two quantities to prevent expert collapse, which would be more useful?

- The dispatch fraction alone is sufficient: just penalize uneven token counts directly
- The probability fraction alone is sufficient: just penalize uneven softmax probabilities directly
- Neither alone is sufficient; you need both quantities working together

::: {.predict-reveal}
**The answer is C.** Neither quantity alone can solve the problem. The dispatch fraction $f_i$ perfectly describes the actual imbalance, but it is computed through an argmax and indicator function, so it has zero gradients. You cannot backpropagate through it. The probability fraction $P_i$ is differentiable (softmax is smooth), but it can be gamed: the router can assign high probability to an expert on a few tokens while actually routing most tokens elsewhere via the argmax. The multiplication $f_i \cdot P_i$ fuses the "what actually happened" signal ($f_i$) with the "what we can optimize" signal ($P_i$) into a single quantity that is both informative and differentiable. The next subsection explains exactly how this works.
:::

:::

### Why the Multiplication Works (The Deep Insight)

Four ideas explain why this simple product solves the load-balancing problem.

**1. The two vectors live in different worlds.** The $f$-vector lives in the discrete world: it counts actual token assignments, and its values jump discontinuously as assignments change. The $P$-vector lives in the continuous world: it averages softmax probabilities, and its values change smoothly as router weights change. Neither vector alone is sufficient for optimization.

**2. The product creates a differentiable loss whose gradient magnitude is controlled by the discrete count.** When you compute $\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} / \partial \theta$ (where $\theta$ are the router parameters), the gradient flows through $P_i$ because softmax is differentiable. The term $f_i$ acts as a constant scaling factor during backpropagation: it is treated as a fixed value, not a function of $\theta$. The result is that if expert $i$ has a high dispatch fraction ($f_i$ is large), the gradient pushing down $P_i$ is large. If expert $i$ has a low dispatch fraction, the gradient is small.

**3. The scaling targets exactly the right experts.** An overloaded expert (high $f_i$) contributes a large term to the loss, generating a strong gradient that pushes the router to reduce $P_i$ for that expert. An underloaded expert (low $f_i$) contributes a small term, so the optimizer focuses its effort on the experts that are actually causing imbalance. The discrete world (actual assignments) controls the gradient magnitude; the continuous world (probabilities) provides the gradient direction.

**4. The loss minimum coincides with uniform routing.** Both $f$ and $P$ are probability distributions: $\sum f_i = 1$ and $\sum P_i = 1$ (with all entries non-negative). Under these constraints, the dot product $\sum f_i P_i$ is minimized when both vectors are uniform: $f_i = P_i = 1/N$ for all $i$. Let us verify this minimum value in concrete numbers.

::: {.exercise-mcq correct="B"}

In the auxiliary load-balancing loss, the gradient of the loss with respect to the router parameters flows through which quantity?

- The dispatch fraction f (the token count fraction), because it directly measures the imbalance
- The probability fraction P (the average softmax probability), because softmax is differentiable
- Both f and P equally, because the loss is their product
- Neither; the loss uses a separate gradient estimator like REINFORCE

::: {.feedback-correct}
Correct. The gradient flows only through P, the average softmax probability. The dispatch fraction f is computed via an argmax and indicator function, which have zero gradient almost everywhere. During backpropagation, f acts as a fixed scaling constant that modulates the gradient magnitude, while P provides the actual gradient direction through the differentiable softmax function.
:::

::: {.feedback-incorrect}
Not quite. Remember: the dispatch fraction f is defined through an indicator function applied to an argmax. The indicator function is flat (zero gradient) almost everywhere and undefined at the boundary. So f cannot provide gradients. The gradient must flow through the differentiable quantity in the product, which is P (the average softmax probability). The term f acts as a constant scaling factor during backpropagation, controlling how strongly the gradient pushes on each expert's probability.
:::

:::

### Why Simpler Alternatives Fail

You might wonder: why not just penalize the $P_i$ values directly, or the $f_i$ values directly? Both approaches have fatal flaws.

**Penalizing only $P_i$ (without $f_i$).** Suppose the loss were $\sum P_i^2$, penalizing any expert with high average probability. The router can game this. It assigns a near-100% softmax score to Expert 3 on a handful of tokens, inflating $P_3$, while actually routing most tokens elsewhere via the argmax. The probabilities look balanced, but the actual token distribution is wildly skewed. The $f_i$ term catches this cheating: it reflects what *actually happened* in the forward pass, not what the router's probabilities *claim* will happen.

**Penalizing only $f_i$ (without $P_i$).** The vector $f_i$ perfectly describes the actual imbalance. But it has zero gradients. The function $\mathbb{1}\{\text{argmax}\; p(x) = i\}$ is flat almost everywhere with respect to the router parameters, so $\partial f_i / \partial \theta = 0$. You cannot backpropagate through an argmax. The optimizer would see a loss value but have no gradient to follow.

Both signals are needed. The $f_i$ vector provides the "what is actually happening" signal; the $P_i$ vector provides the "what we can optimize" signal. The product of these two vectors fuses both roles into a single quantity that is both informative and differentiable.

::: {.exercise-mcq correct="C"}

A colleague proposes a simpler load-balancing loss: just minimize the sum of squared softmax probabilities, i.e., penalize any expert whose average probability P is too high. They argue this avoids the complexity of tracking actual token counts. What is the fatal flaw in this approach?

- It has zero gradients because softmax probabilities are not differentiable
- It is too expensive to compute because it requires iterating over all tokens twice
- The router can "cheat" by assigning high softmax probability to an expert on a few tokens while routing most tokens elsewhere via the argmax, making probabilities look balanced while actual token counts remain skewed
- It only works for top-1 routing and breaks when using top-2 or higher

::: {.feedback-correct}
Exactly. Without the dispatch fraction f to anchor the loss to what actually happened in the forward pass, the router can exploit the gap between probabilities and assignments. It can give Expert 3 near-100% softmax probability on a handful of tokens (inflating P for Expert 3) while the argmax routes most tokens to other experts. The P values look balanced, but the actual token distribution is wildly skewed. The f term catches this cheating because it reflects actual assignment counts.
:::

::: {.feedback-incorrect}
Think about what the router can do when only softmax probabilities are penalized, with no reference to actual token assignments. The softmax probabilities are what the router *claims* will happen. The argmax decisions are what *actually* happens. These can diverge: the router can assign high probability to an expert on a small number of tokens without that expert receiving many tokens via the argmax. This gap between "claimed" and "actual" routing is the fatal flaw. The dispatch fraction f closes this gap by measuring actual assignments.
:::

:::

### Worked Numerical Example

Consider a batch of $T = 8$ tokens routed across $N = 4$ experts. Suppose the routing produced an imbalanced assignment.

**Imbalanced scenario.** Expert 1 receives 4 tokens, Expert 2 receives 2, Expert 3 receives 2, Expert 4 receives 0. The dispatch fractions are $f = [0.5, 0.25, 0.25, 0.0]$. Meanwhile, the average softmax probabilities across the batch are $P = [0.4, 0.2, 0.3, 0.1]$. The auxiliary loss is:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = \alpha \cdot 4 \cdot (0.5 \times 0.4 + 0.25 \times 0.2 + 0.25 \times 0.3 + 0.0 \times 0.1)
$$

$$
= \alpha \cdot 4 \cdot (0.20 + 0.05 + 0.075 + 0.0) = \alpha \cdot 4 \cdot 0.325 = 1.3\alpha
$$

![Imbalanced routing: FFNN 1 receives the majority of tokens while other experts sit idle. The router probabilities (bar charts) show how the routing decision concentrates on a single expert for most input tokens. Source: Maarten Grootendorst, "A Visual Guide to Mixture of Experts" (2024).](Mixture of Experts/images/grootendorst-imbalanced-routing.png){#fig-imbalanced-routing}

**Balanced scenario.** Each expert receives exactly 2 tokens, so $f = [0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25]$. The probabilities are also uniform: $P = [0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25]$. The loss is:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = \alpha \cdot 4 \cdot (4 \times 0.25 \times 0.25) = \alpha \cdot 4 \cdot 0.25 = 1.0\alpha
$$

The balanced case gives a lower loss: $1.0\alpha < 1.3\alpha$. The optimizer is incentivized to move toward balance. In general, the minimum of $\sum f_i P_i$ subject to $\sum f_i = 1$ and $\sum P_i = 1$ (with non-negative entries) is $1/N$, achieved when both vectors are uniform. You can prove this by applying the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. More directly, observe that $\sum f_i P_i$ is the inner product of two vectors on the probability simplex. The inner product is minimized when the vectors are "as orthogonal as possible," which on the simplex corresponds to the uniform distribution.

Notice the gradient dynamics in the imbalanced case. Expert 1 has the largest product ($0.5 \times 0.4 = 0.20$), so the gradient pushes hardest to reduce $P_1$, the average probability the router gives to Expert 1. Expert 4 contributes zero to the loss ($0.0 \times 0.1 = 0$), so no gradient pressure acts on $P_4$ through this term. The optimizer naturally focuses its effort where the imbalance is worst.

::: {.exercise-fillin}

Try a variation of the worked example. A batch of tokens is routed across N = 4 experts, producing dispatch fractions f = [0.5, 0.0, 0.25, 0.25] and average softmax probabilities P = [0.3, 0.1, 0.4, 0.2]. Use alpha = 0.01.

1. Compute each product: f1 times P1 = 0.5 times 0.3 = 0.15
2. f2 times P2 = 0.0 times 0.1 = 0.00
3. f3 times P3 = 0.25 times 0.4 = 0.10
4. f4 times P4 = 0.25 times 0.2 = 0.05
5. The sum of all four products equals {B|A: 0.20|B: 0.30|C: 0.40}
6. Multiply by alpha times N: the final auxiliary loss equals 0.01 times 4 times 0.30 = {B|A: 0.008|B: 0.012|C: 0.024}

::: {.fillin-feedback}
**Step 5: The sum is 0.15 + 0.00 + 0.10 + 0.05 = 0.30 (answer B).** Step 6: The final loss is 0.01 times 4 times 0.30 = 0.012 (answer B). Compare this to the perfectly balanced case where the loss equals alpha = 0.01. The imbalanced scenario produces a higher loss (0.012 > 0.01), confirming the optimizer is incentivized toward balance. Also notice that Expert 2 receives zero tokens (f2 = 0), so it contributes nothing to the loss and receives no gradient pressure through this term, even though its average probability P2 = 0.1 is nonzero.
:::

:::

### The Scaling Factor and $\alpha$

Two details about the loss formulation deserve attention.

The coefficient $\alpha$ controls the strength of the load-balancing pressure relative to the primary task loss (language modeling, translation, or whatever the model is trained for). [Fedus et al. (JMLR 2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961) used $\alpha = 10^{-2}$ in Switch Transformers. Getting this value right is a balancing act:

- Too large: the auxiliary loss dominates the total loss. The model learns to balance tokens perfectly across experts but neglects the actual task. Every expert handles the same mix of token types, and specialization vanishes.
- Too small: the auxiliary loss is too weak to overcome the self-reinforcing dynamics of expert collapse. One expert still hogs most tokens.

The factor $N$ in $\alpha \cdot N \cdot \sum f_i P_i$ serves a normalization purpose. As you increase the number of experts, the minimum value of $\sum f_i P_i$ decreases (it equals $1/N$ at the uniform optimum). Multiplying by $N$ keeps the loss at the optimum equal to $\alpha$ regardless of expert count. Without this factor, the loss would shrink as $N$ grows, and you would need to increase $\alpha$ every time you added more experts.

::: {.callout-warning}

**Common Misconception: The auxiliary loss directly optimizes the token counts $f_i$.**

That claim is wrong. The $f_i$ values are non-differentiable. They are computed from indicator functions applied to argmax outputs. No gradient flows through $f_i$. During backpropagation, the gradient of $\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}}$ flows *only* through the $P_i$ values (the differentiable softmax averages). The $f_i$ values act as scaling factors that modulate gradient magnitude, not as optimization targets. The auxiliary loss nudges the router probabilities $P_i$ in a direction that indirectly changes the token assignments $f_i$ on the *next* forward pass. The influence is two-step: the loss adjusts probabilities now, and those adjusted probabilities change the argmax decisions later.

:::

::: {.callout-note}

**Think Hard: At what point does too much balance hurt model quality?**

The auxiliary loss pushes toward uniform routing, but the task loss pushes toward routing tokens to the best expert for the job. If $\alpha$ is too large, the balance pressure dominates, and every expert handles the same mix of tokens. Specialization dies. The model routes "bank" and "the" and "property" all to the same set of experts, indiscriminately.

You can detect over-balancing by monitoring per-expert token distributions during training. If every expert's distribution of token types is identical (the same mix of nouns, verbs, punctuation, domain-specific terms), the model is over-balanced. Healthy MoE training shows experts developing distinct preferences: one expert might handle function words, another might handle named entities, a third might handle numerical expressions.

The 2025 paper "Demons in the Detail" ([Qiu et al., 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.11873)) revealed a subtler version of this problem. They showed that computing the load-balancing loss per *micro-batch* (the small batch on each GPU) rather than per *global batch* (the full batch across all GPUs) aggressively inhibits specialization.

The reason: micro-batches are small, so the $f_i$ counts are noisy. A micro-batch of 32 tokens across 8 experts gives each expert roughly 4 tokens; random variation in such small counts generates large, noisy gradients that wash out any genuine specialization signal. Global-batch computation produces much more stable $f_i$ values, allowing the model to balance at the corpus level while still specializing within domains.

:::

Beyond the load-balancing loss, large-scale MoE training requires a separate stabilization technique called *router z-loss*, introduced in ST-MoE ([Zoph et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.08906)). During training, router logits can grow unboundedly large. When these large logits pass through softmax, they cause numerical instability: gradients spike or vanish, and training can collapse. Router z-loss penalizes large router logits directly, keeping the gating network well-behaved:

$$
\mathcal{L}_z = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{x \in \mathcal{B}} \log^2 \left( \sum_{i=1}^{N} e^{h_i(x)} \right)
$$

Here $h_i(x)$ are the router logits. The penalty is distinct from the $f_i \cdot P_i$ load-balancing loss and is added alongside it. ST-MoE found that router z-loss was critical for stable training at 269B parameters.

The $f_i \cdot P_i$ loss formulation, elegant as it is, addresses only one side of the systems challenge. Even with balanced routing, MoE layers face a hard engineering constraint: each expert can only process a limited number of tokens per forward pass. When an expert receives more tokens than it can handle, something must give. In the next section, we turn to capacity factors, token dropping, and the systems-level view of making MoE work in practice.
